question: What are the main HTTP methods and what is each used for?
title: HTTP Methods Overview
direct_answer: The main HTTP methods are GET (retrieve data), POST (create new resources), PUT (replace entire resource), PATCH (partial update), and DELETE (remove resource). Each maps to a CRUD operation and has specific idempotency and safety characteristics that determine how clients and proxies can safely use them.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the semantic contract of each HTTP method and can map them to real CRUD operations in a REST API.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using POST for all write operations or claiming PUT and PATCH are the same thing.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the idempotency guarantee of each method and give a concrete example of why GET must never modify state.

sections.title: HTTP Methods as the Verbs of REST
sections.content:
HTTP methods define **what action** a client wants to perform on a resource. Think of them as verbs in a sentence where the URL is the noun. **GET** retrieves data without changing anything—like viewing a product page. **POST** creates something new—like submitting an order form. **PUT** replaces an entire resource—like overwriting a user profile with new data. **PATCH** updates specific fields—like changing just the email address. **DELETE** removes a resource—like canceling an order.

Each method has a **contract** that determines how servers, browsers, and proxies treat the request. GET is **safe** (no side effects) and **idempotent** (repeatable), so browsers can prefetch GET requests. POST is neither—each POST creates a new resource, so retrying it causes duplicates. PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe—calling DELETE twice still results in the resource being gone. Understanding these contracts prevents bugs like using GET to delete data (breaking the safe contract) or using POST for updates (losing idempotency benefits).

sections.title: Spring Boot REST Controller with All HTTP Methods
When to Use Each HTTP Method
sections.content:
Use **GET** when fetching data that already exists—product listings, user profiles, order history. Never use GET to trigger actions like deleting or updating.

Use **POST** when creating something entirely new where the server assigns the ID—submitting a registration form, placing an order, uploading a file.

Use **PUT** when the client knows the full resource representation and wants to replace everything—updating a user profile where you send all fields including unchanged ones.

Use **PATCH** when updating just a few fields without touching the rest—changing a user's email or an order's status.

Use **DELETE** when removing a resource permanently—canceling a subscription, deleting a comment. In a mobile app calling your Spring Boot API, GET is for screen loads, POST for form submissions, PATCH for toggle switches or single-field edits, and DELETE for user-initiated removals.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using POST for everything**: Freshers often default to POST for all operations because it accepts a request body, losing the semantic meaning and caching benefits of other methods.
- **Modifying state with GET**: Implementing a delete or update operation with GET breaks the safe method contract—browsers might prefetch the URL and accidentally trigger the action.
- **Confusing PUT and PATCH**: Using PUT to update a single field requires sending the entire resource; omitted fields get nulled out, causing data loss.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **GET**: retrieves data, safe and idempotent, no request body, cacheable by browsers and proxies
**POST**: creates new resources, not idempotent, each call creates a duplicate, returns 201 Created with Location header
**PUT**: replaces entire resource, idempotent, requires sending all fields, omitted fields become null
**PATCH**: updates specific fields, idempotent, only sends changed fields, safer than PUT for partial updates
**DELETE**: removes resource, idempotent, second call returns 404 but server state unchanged
**Safe methods**: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS never modify state, allowing aggressive caching and prefetching
**Idempotent methods**: GET, PUT, PATCH, DELETE produce same server state when repeated, enabling safe retries

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The main HTTP methods are GET for reading data, POST for creating new resources, PUT for replacing an entire resource, PATCH for partial updates, and DELETE for removing resources. Each one maps to a CRUD operation. GET is safe and idempotent, meaning it doesn't change anything on the server and you can call it multiple times without side effects. That's why browsers can prefetch GET requests or cache them aggressively. POST isn't idempotent because each call creates a new resource. If you retry a failed POST, you might create duplicate orders. PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe. Calling DELETE twice still results in the resource being deleted once. The second call returns 404 but the server state is the same. PUT replaces the whole resource, so if you don't send a field it gets nulled out. PATCH updates just the fields you specify. The distinction matters because mobile apps rely on idempotency to safely retry failed requests without duplicating data. A common mistake freshers make is using POST for updates or using GET to trigger deletions. That breaks the HTTP contract and causes bugs when browsers or proxies interact with your API. In Spring Boot, you map these with at-GetMapping, at-PostMapping, at-PutMapping, at-PatchMapping, and at-DeleteMapping annotations on controller methods.

question: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
title: PUT vs PATCH
direct_answer: PUT replaces the entire resource with what you send—any field not included becomes null or its default value. PATCH updates only the fields you specify, leaving others unchanged. Use PATCH for partial updates to avoid accidentally clearing fields the client didn't mean to modify.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the semantic difference and can choose the right method for partial updates.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using PUT for partial updates and accidentally nulling out fields, or thinking PATCH is always better than PUT.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention JSON Patch (RFC 6902) for complex partial updates and explain when full replacement with PUT is actually safer.

sections.title: PUT Replaces, PATCH Updates
sections.content:
The key difference is **scope of change**. **PUT** performs a **full replacement**—you send the complete resource representation, and the server overwrites everything. Any field you don't include gets set to null or its default value.

Think of it like rewriting a file. **PATCH** performs a **partial update**—you send only the fields you want to change, and the server updates just those, leaving everything else intact.

Think of it like using find-and-replace on specific lines. If you have a User with email, name, and address, a PUT requires sending all three fields. If you omit address, it becomes null. A PATCH lets you send just email, and name and address remain unchanged. Both are **idempotent**—applying the same update twice results in the same final state. The choice depends on your use case: use PATCH when clients update one or two fields frequently (like toggling a setting) to avoid the overhead and risk of sending the entire resource. Use PUT when you want the **replace semantics** to be explicit, ensuring the resource exactly matches what the client sent.

sections.title: When to Use PUT vs PATCH
sections.content:
Use **PUT** when the client has the complete resource and wants to replace it entirely—like editing a user profile where the form displays all fields and submits everything. PUT is safer when you want **explicit replacement semantics**: if the client doesn't send a field, you want it gone.

Use **PATCH** when clients update individual fields frequently without loading the full resource—like a mobile app toggling a notification setting or updating order status. PATCH reduces payload size and avoids race conditions where one client's PUT overwrites another client's concurrent changes to different fields. In a Spring Boot API serving a mobile app, use PATCH for single-field updates like changing email or enabling dark mode.

Use PUT for admin panels where you edit and save entire entities. For complex updates like reordering items in a list or conditional changes, use **JSON Patch** (RFC 6902), which sends an array of operations like add, remove, replace with paths.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using PUT for partial updates**: Freshers send a PUT with just the email field, not realizing the server nulls out name and address because they weren't included. This causes data loss.
- **Thinking PATCH is always better**: For full-form submissions where all fields are present, PUT is simpler and more explicit—PATCH adds complexity without benefit.
- **Not validating PATCH fields**: Accepting a PATCH that updates a field to null when null isn't valid, or allowing updates to immutable fields like createdAt without server-side checks.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: PUT and PATCH both update resources but they work differently. PUT replaces the entire resource with what you send. If you have a User with email, name, and address, and you PUT with just email and name, the address becomes null because you didn't include it. PUT is like rewriting a file completely. PATCH updates only the fields you specify and leaves everything else unchanged. You can PATCH just the email and the name and address stay the same. Both are idempotent, meaning calling them twice with the same data results in the same final state. You'd use PUT when the client has the complete resource and wants to replace it, like submitting a full edit form. You'd use PATCH when updating just one or two fields, like changing an order status or toggling a setting in a mobile app. PATCH reduces payload size and avoids accidentally clearing fields. A common mistake is using PUT for partial updates and not sending all the fields. That causes data loss because omitted fields get nulled out. Another mistake is thinking PATCH is always better. For full-form submissions, PUT is actually simpler and more explicit. There's also JSON Patch, which is RFC 6902, that lets you send an array of operations like add or remove on specific JSON paths. That's useful for complex updates like reordering lists.

question: How do you map HTTP methods to Spring Boot controller annotations?
title: HTTP Methods in Spring Boot
direct_answer: Spring Boot provides @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @PatchMapping, and @DeleteMapping to map HTTP methods to controller methods. These are shortcuts for @RequestMapping with a specific method parameter. Use @PathVariable for URL segments and @RequestParam for query parameters.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Spring Boot knowledge—can you write a REST controller that correctly uses HTTP methods?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @PostMapping for reads or updates, or not knowing @GetMapping can't accept a request body.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show proper use of ResponseEntity with correct status codes (201 for POST, 204 for DELETE) and explain @PathVariable vs @RequestParam.

sections.title: Spring Boot Annotations for HTTP Methods
sections.content:
Spring Boot provides **specialized annotations** that map HTTP methods to controller methods: **@GetMapping**, **@PostMapping**, **@PutMapping**, **@PatchMapping**, and **@DeleteMapping**. These are shorthand for **@RequestMapping** with a method attribute—@GetMapping is the same as @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET).

Use **@PathVariable** to extract values from the URL path, like /orders/{id} where id becomes a method parameter. Use **@RequestParam** for query parameters, like /orders?status=SHIPPED. Use **@RequestBody** to deserialize JSON from the request body into a Java object. GET and DELETE typically don't have request bodies. POST, PUT, and PATCH do. Return **ResponseEntity** to control the HTTP status code and headers—return ResponseEntity.ok(data) for 200, ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(data) for 201, ResponseEntity.noContent().build() for 204. The framework automatically serializes your return value to JSON using Jackson. These annotations make REST controllers concise and declarative—you're explicitly stating the HTTP method contract right in the annotation.

emerald|@PutMapping|~maps PUT requests, for full replacement, use @PathVariable for ID and @RequestBody for full...
violet|@PatchMapping|~maps PATCH requests, for partial updates, use @RequestParam or @RequestBody for changed fields

sections.title: Complete REST Controller with All HTTP Methods
When to Use Each Annotation
sections.content:
Use **@GetMapping** for all read operations—listing resources, fetching by ID, search and filtering with query parameters. Never use it for operations that modify state.

Use **@PostMapping** when creating new resources where the server assigns the ID—user registration, placing orders, uploading files. Return 201 Created with a Location header pointing to the new resource.

Use **@PutMapping** for full replacement updates where the client sends the complete resource. The ID is in the path variable. Return 200 OK with the updated resource or 204 No Content.

Use **@PatchMapping** for partial updates like changing email or status. You can use @RequestParam for simple single-field updates or @RequestBody with a DTO containing only changed fields.

Use **@DeleteMapping** to remove resources. Return 204 No Content on success or 404 Not Found if the resource doesn't exist. Always use **@PathVariable** for resource identifiers in the URL path and **@RequestParam** for optional filters or single-field updates.

Use **@RequestBody** for complex payloads that need to be deserialized from JSON.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @PostMapping for reads**: Freshers sometimes use POST for queries because they want to send a complex search filter. This breaks REST semantics and prevents caching. Use GET with query parameters instead.
- **Forgetting @PathVariable or @RequestParam**: Defining a method parameter but not annotating it, causing Spring to fail to bind it.
- **Using @RequestBody with GET**: GET requests don't have bodies by HTTP spec. Trying to use at-RequestBody with at-GetMapping causes errors.
- **Returning wrong status codes**: Returning 200 OK for a POST that creates a resource instead of 201 Created, or returning 200 for a DELETE instead of 204 No Content.
- **Not handling missing resources**: Not checking if a resource exists before updating or deleting, causing NullPointerException instead of returning 404.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **@GetMapping**: maps GET requests, for reads only, use @PathVariable for ID and @RequestParam for filters
**@PostMapping**: maps POST requests, for creating resources, use @RequestBody for JSON, return 201 Created
**@PutMapping**: maps PUT requests, for full replacement, use @PathVariable for ID and @RequestBody for full resource
**@PatchMapping**: maps PATCH requests, for partial updates, use @RequestParam or @RequestBody for changed fields
**@DeleteMapping**: maps DELETE requests, for removing resources, return 204 No Content on success
**@PathVariable**: extracts values from URL path like /customers/{id}, required by default
**@RequestParam**: extracts query parameters like ?status=ACTIVE, can be optional with required=false
**ResponseEntity**: lets you control status code and headers, use ResponseEntity.ok(), status(), notFound(), noContent()

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Spring Boot provides specialized annotations for mapping HTTP methods to controller methods. You have at-GetMapping for GET requests, at-PostMapping for POST, at-PutMapping for PUT, at-PatchMapping for PATCH, and at-DeleteMapping for DELETE. These are just shortcuts for at-RequestMapping with a method parameter, but they're more concise. You use at-PathVariable to extract values from the URL path, like when you have /orders/123 and you want to get the 123 as a method parameter. You use at-RequestParam for query parameters, like ?status=SHIPPED. For POST, PUT, and PATCH, you use at-RequestBody to deserialize the JSON from the request into a Java object. GET and DELETE typically don't have request bodies. You should return ResponseEntity to control the status code. Use ResponseEntity.ok for 200, ResponseEntity.status HttpStatus.CREATED for 201 when creating, and ResponseEntity.noContent for 204 when deleting. A common mistake freshers make is using at-PostMapping for read operations or trying to use at-RequestBody with at-GetMapping, which doesn't work because GET requests don't have bodies. Another mistake is returning the wrong status codes, like 200 for everything instead of 201 for creates or 204 for deletes. You should also check if a resource exists before updating or deleting it and return 404 Not Found if it doesn't, instead of letting a NullPointerException happen.

question: What is idempotency and which HTTP methods are idempotent?
title: Idempotency in HTTP Methods
direct_answer: Idempotency means making the same request multiple times produces the same server state as making it once. GET, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE are idempotent by specification. POST is not idempotent—each POST creates a new resource. This matters for retry logic in distributed systems.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you grasp the practical implications of idempotency for building resilient REST APIs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Claiming PATCH is not idempotent or thinking idempotency means returning the same response body every time.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why POST isn't idempotent and how mobile apps use idempotency to safely retry failed requests without duplicate side effects.

sections.title: Idempotency: Safe to Retry Without Duplication
sections.content:
**Idempotency** means that calling the same operation multiple times leaves the server in the **same state** as calling it once. It's not about getting the same response body—it's about the **effect on server data**.

Think of a light switch: flipping it to ON multiple times still results in the light being on. **GET** is idempotent because reading data ten times doesn't change it. **PUT** is idempotent because replacing a resource with the same data twice still results in that data being stored once. **DELETE** is idempotent because deleting a resource twice still results in it being deleted—the second call returns 404 but the state is identical. **PATCH** is idempotent when the update operation itself is idempotent—setting status to SHIPPED twice results in SHIPPED. **POST** is **not idempotent** because each call creates a new resource. Submitting an order form twice creates two orders with different IDs. This matters in real systems: when a mobile app's network request times out, it doesn't know if the server processed it. If the operation is idempotent, the app can safely retry. If it's POST, retrying risks creating duplicates unless you add extra logic like idempotency keys.

sections.title: Idempotent vs Non-Idempotent Operations
When Idempotency Matters
sections.content: Idempotency is critical when **network reliability is uncertain**—mobile apps on spotty connections, distributed microservices communicating across data centers, webhook retries after failures. If a mobile client sends a PATCH request to update order status and the request times out, the app doesn't know if the server processed it. Because PATCH is idempotent, the app can safely retry without checking—calling it again won't create duplicate state changes. For POST requests that create resources, you need an **idempotency key** pattern: the client generates a unique UUID and sends it in a header. The server stores this key and refuses to process duplicate requests with the same key, returning the original response instead. Payment APIs like Stripe require idempotency keys on all POST endpoints to prevent duplicate charges when clients retry failed transactions. Without idempotency guarantees, you'd need complex reconciliation logic or risk data corruption from retries.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing idempotency with identical responses**: Freshers think idempotent means getting the exact same JSON back, but it actually means the server state is the same. Deleting a resource twice returns 404 the second time but is still idempotent.
- **Claiming PATCH isn't idempotent**: PATCH is idempotent by specification—updating email to alice at example.com twice results in that email being set once.
- **Implementing non-idempotent PUT**: If your PUT endpoint increments a counter or appends to a list instead of replacing, you've broken the idempotency contract and created subtle retry bugs.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Idempotency**: making the same request N times produces the same server state as making it once
**GET, PUT, PATCH, DELETE**: all idempotent by HTTP specification, safe to retry without side effects
**POST**: not idempotent, each call creates a new resource with a new ID, retries cause duplicates
**Response bodies can differ**: DELETE returns 200 first time and 404 second time, still idempotent because state is identical
**Idempotency keys**: make POST idempotent by having client send a UUID header, server deduplicates using it
**Network timeouts**: idempotency allows mobile apps to retry timed-out requests safely without checking server state first
**Implementation requirement**: your code must ensure repeated calls don't accumulate side effects like incrementing counters or creating duplicates

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Idempotency means making the same request multiple times produces the same server state as making it once. It's not about getting identical responses, it's about the effect on your data. GET, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE are all idempotent. POST is not. If you call GET five times, you're reading the same data five times, nothing changes. If you call DELETE twice, the resource is deleted once. The second call returns 404 but the state is the same as after the first call. That's still idempotent. PUT replaces a resource, so replacing it twice with the same data results in it being stored once. PATCH updates specific fields, and updating them twice to the same value results in that value being set once. POST isn't idempotent because each call creates a new resource. If you POST an order and retry it due to a network timeout, you'll create two orders with different IDs. This matters a lot in mobile apps. When a request times out, the app doesn't know if the server processed it. For idempotent methods, the app can just retry safely. For POST, you need an idempotency key pattern where the client sends a UUID in a header and the server deduplicates. A common mistake is thinking idempotency means the response is identical every time. It doesn't. It means the server state is identical after repeated calls.

speakable_v2.hook: Idempotent means you can hit the same endpoint ten times and the outcome is identical to hitting it once — that's what makes retries safe.

beats.text: Idempotency means calling the same operation multiple times produces the same end state as calling it once. It's a promise about repeatability. GET, PUT, DELETE, and (when correctly implemented) PATCH are idempotent. POST is not.

Networks fail. A client that doesn't know if its request reached the server needs to retry. If the operation is idempotent, retrying is safe. If it isn't — like POST creating an order — retrying may charge the customer twice. Idempotency is the foundation of safe retry logic.

items: GET: idempotent and safe — reading a task list 100 times gives the same list
PUT: idempotent — replacing task 42 with the same body 100 times leaves the same task
DELETE: idempotent — first call removes the task and returns 200; later calls return 404, but the end state (task gone) is identical
POST: not idempotent — calling POST /tasks 100 times creates 100 tasks
PATCH: idempotent if your implementation merges cleanly; can become non-idempotent if it appends rather than replaces

beats.text: Payment scenario: user clicks Pay twice due to a slow network. If your payment endpoint is POST /payments, you may charge twice. The fix is an Idempotency-Key header — the client sends a unique key; the server stores the result for that key and returns the same response on duplicates. Stripe uses exactly this pattern. non-obvious: idempotency is about the end state, not the HTTP response code. DELETE returning 404 the second time is still idempotent — the resource is gone either way.

items: Saying PATCH is always non-idempotent — it depends on your implementation; a merge-patch is idempotent
Thinking idempotency means same response code — it means same end state; DELETE returning 404 on a repeat is still idempotent

speakable_v2.cap: Idempotent = same end state no matter how many times you call it. GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent. POST is not. Use Idempotency-Key headers to make POST safe to retry.

question: What are safe HTTP methods and why does the distinction matter?
title: Safe HTTP Methods
direct_answer: Safe HTTP methods are GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS—methods that only read data and never modify server state. The distinction matters because browsers and proxies can cache, prefetch, or retry safe methods without side effects, but must treat unsafe methods (POST, PUT, DELETE) cautiously.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the contract between HTTP methods and intermediaries like browsers, proxies, and CDNs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing safe with idempotent—DELETE is idempotent but not safe because it modifies state.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how browsers use the safe property to decide whether to preload links or cache responses aggressively.

sections.title: Safe Methods: Read-Only by Contract
sections.content:
A **safe HTTP method** is one that **does not modify server state**—it's read-only. The three safe methods are **GET** (retrieve a resource), **HEAD** (retrieve headers without body), and **OPTIONS** (query allowed methods).

The critical insight is that this is a **contract** between your API and HTTP clients. When you mark an endpoint as GET, you're promising that calling it won't change data, create resources, or trigger side effects. This promise lets **browsers prefetch** GET requests to speed up page loads, lets **proxies and CDNs cache** responses aggressively, and lets clients **retry** failed requests without fear. If you violate this contract—like using GET to delete a resource—browsers might prefetch the URL while hovering over a link and accidentally trigger the deletion. **Safe is not the same as idempotent**. **DELETE** is idempotent (deleting twice leaves the same final state) but not safe (it modifies state). **GET** is both safe and idempotent. Unsafe methods (**POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE**) require explicit user action like clicking a button—browsers won't prefetch them automatically.

sections.title: Safe vs Unsafe Methods in Spring Boot
When the Safe Property Matters
sections.content: The safe property matters when your API interacts with **intermediaries**—browsers, proxies, CDNs, web crawlers. Browsers use the safe property to decide whether to **prefetch links** when users hover over them, improving perceived performance. They also use it to decide whether clicking Back needs to re-fetch the page or can use a cached version. CDNs aggressively cache safe methods but not unsafe ones—a GET request might be served from a cache in Singapore without hitting your server, but a POST always goes to origin. Web crawlers like Googlebot only follow safe methods to avoid triggering actions while indexing your site. If you implement a delete operation as GET, a crawler could accidentally delete your data. In mobile apps calling your Spring Boot API, the safe property determines whether the OS-level network stack can automatically retry requests after connectivity is restored. Safe methods get retried; unsafe methods require user confirmation. Always use GET for reads, never for writes or actions.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using GET for actions**: Implementing delete or update as GET because it's easier to test in a browser URL bar. This violates the safe contract and causes browsers or crawlers to trigger unintended actions.
- **Confusing safe with idempotent**: Thinking DELETE is safe because you can call it twice. DELETE is idempotent but not safe—it modifies state, so browsers won't prefetch it.
- **Ignoring HEAD and OPTIONS**: Not implementing HEAD (which should return the same headers as GET without a body) or OPTIONS (for CORS preflight), breaking compatibility with browsers and tools that expect these safe methods to work.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Safe methods**: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS—read-only, never modify server state, safe for intermediaries to prefetch and cache
**Unsafe methods**: POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE—modify state, require explicit user action, not cached or prefetched
**Browser prefetching**: browsers prefetch safe method URLs on hover to speed up page loads, would trigger unintended actions if GET modifies state
**CDN caching**: CDNs cache safe methods aggressively, reducing origin server load, but never cache unsafe methods
**Safe vs idempotent**: DELETE is idempotent but not safe (modifies state), GET is both safe and idempotent
**Web crawlers**: only follow safe methods to avoid triggering actions, using GET for deletes risks data loss from crawlers
**Contract violation**: implementing actions as GET breaks HTTP semantics and causes subtle bugs with browsers, proxies, and tools

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Safe HTTP methods are GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS. They only read data and never modify server state. The distinction matters because it's a contract between your API and HTTP clients like browsers, proxies, and CDNs. When you use GET, you're promising that calling it won't change anything on the server. That lets browsers prefetch GET requests while you hover over a link to make pages load faster. It lets CDNs cache GET responses aggressively without worrying about serving stale data after a write. It lets web crawlers follow GET links without accidentally triggering actions. If you violate this contract by using GET to delete a resource, a crawler or browser prefetch could trigger the deletion without the user intending it. Safe is different from idempotent. DELETE is idempotent because calling it twice leaves the same final state, but it's not safe because it modifies state. GET is both safe and idempotent. Unsafe methods are POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE. Browsers won't prefetch these automatically. They require explicit user action like clicking a submit button. A common mistake freshers make is using GET for delete or update operations because it's easier to test by typing a URL in the browser. That breaks the safe method contract and causes bugs when browsers or CDNs interact with your API. Always use GET for reads only, never for writes or actions.

speakable_v2.hook: Safe methods don't change server state — browsers and proxies exploit that promise in ways that affect your app.

beats.text: A safe HTTP method is one that doesn't modify server state. GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS are safe. Calling them has no side effects — nothing is created, updated, or deleted. All safe methods are also idempotent, but not all idempotent methods are safe.

Browsers, crawlers, and proxies treat safe methods as read-only. A browser can preload a linked page with GET without concern. A proxy can cache GET responses. If GET could trigger a delete, the web would break every time a search engine crawled your site.

items: Safe and idempotent: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS — read-only; no state change; cacheable
Idempotent but not safe: PUT, DELETE — change state but safely repeatable
Not safe, not idempotent: POST — changes state and calling twice may create duplicates
PATCH: idempotent if correctly implemented, but not safe — it modifies state

beats.text: In our task app, GET /tasks is safe — a browser can fetch it on every page load and cache it freely. POST /tasks is not safe — a browser will warn before replaying it on refresh because replaying could create a duplicate task. CSRF attacks target unsafe methods (POST, PUT, DELETE) because a forged request that triggers a GET causes no damage, but a forged POST could create or change data. Spring Security's CSRF protection only guards unsafe methods for this reason. production trap: some devs put data-changing logic behind GET endpoints for convenience — that breaks caching, makes bookmarks dangerous, and is a CSRF risk.

items: Confusing safe with idempotent — safe is a subset of idempotent; all safe are idempotent, not vice versa
Putting data-changing logic in GET endpoints — proxies may cache them, and browsers may prefetch them silently

speakable_v2.cap: Safe = no state change. GET, HEAD, OPTIONS are safe. All safe methods are idempotent — but idempotent doesn't mean safe. Browsers and caches rely on the safe guarantee.
